```{r}
#| include: false
source("assets/setup.R")
source("assets/quiz.R")
# complete cases incl. waist (used in the model-building demos)
cc <- ncd |> drop_na(sbp, salt_g, age, bmi, waist, sex, residence, education, tobacco, alcohol, phys_act)
m_crude <- lm(sbp ~ salt_g, data = cc)
m_adj   <- lm(sbp ~ salt_g + age + bmi + sex + residence + education + tobacco + alcohol + phys_act, data = cc)
b_c <- coef(m_crude)[["salt_g"]]; b_a <- coef(m_adj)[["salt_g"]]
ci_a <- confint(m_adj)["salt_g", ]
```

## Where we are

::: {.incremental}
- Session 2: one predictor → slope in units, prediction, R²
- Today: **is the slope real? is it confounded? how do we build a defensible model?**
  - Test and estimate β: **p-values and confidence intervals**
  - **Statistical vs clinical** significance
  - **Confounding** and adjustment — crude vs adjusted β
  - **Dummy coding** of categorical predictors
  - **Model-building strategies** — and why stepwise is risky
:::

# Topic 5 — Inference for β {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Is the slope different from zero?

::: {.key}
**H₀:** β = 0 (no linear association)   **H₁:** β ≠ 0
:::

```{r}
tidy(m_crude, conf.int = TRUE) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ signif(.x, 3)))
```

::: {.incremental}
- **t = estimate ÷ standard error** — how many SEs from zero
- **p-value** — if H₀ were true, the chance of a |t| this large or larger
- **95% CI** = estimate ± ≈2 SE
:::

## What a p-value looks like

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.1
t_obs <- summary(m_adj)$coefficients["alcoholYes", "t value"]
dfr <- df.residual(m_adj)
xs <- seq(-4.5, 4.5, length.out = 400)
d  <- tibble(x = xs, y = dt(xs, dfr))
ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(data = filter(d, x >= abs(t_obs)), fill = col_red, alpha = .5) +
  geom_area(data = filter(d, x <= -abs(t_obs)), fill = col_red, alpha = .5) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = col_navy) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1) * t_obs, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 2.2, y = .25, hjust = 0, size = 5.5,
           label = paste0("Alcohol: t = ", round(t_obs, 2), "\np = ", signif(2 * pt(-abs(t_obs), dfr), 2),
                          "\n(shaded tails)")) +
  labs(x = "t statistic if the true β were 0", y = "density")
```

## What a p-value is — and is not

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.good}
**It is**

the probability of data this extreme **if β were truly 0** (and the model assumptions hold)
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.bad}
**It is not**

- the probability that H₀ is true
- the size or importance of the effect
- a measure of whether the finding will replicate
:::
:::
:::

## Confidence intervals say more

```{r}
cbind(estimate = coef(m_adj), confint(m_adj))["salt_g", ] |> round(2)
```

::: {.incremental}
- Adjusted salt effect: **`r round(b_a, 1)` mmHg per g/day** (95% CI **`r round(ci_a[1], 1)` to `r round(ci_a[2], 1)`**)
- A CI shows **size** *and* **precision**; p only says whether 0 is excluded
- CI excludes 0 ⇔ p < 0.05 (same information, richer format)
:::

## Statistical vs clinical significance

```{r}
# A tiny true effect: 0.5 mmHg per g/day, SD of salt = 2.3 g, residual SD = 15 mmHg
tibble(n = c(50, 200, 1000, 5000, 20000)) |>
  mutate(se = 15 / (2.3 * sqrt(n)), t = 0.5 / se, p = 2 * pt(-abs(t), n - 2)) |>
  mutate(across(c(se, t), ~ round(.x, 2)), p = signif(p, 2))
```

::: {.warn}
With enough people, even an effect of **0.5 mmHg per g/day** becomes "highly significant". Ask two separate questions: **Is it unlikely to be chance?** (p) and **Is it big enough to matter for patients or programmes?** (effect size + CI).
:::

::: {.notes}
Our adjusted effect is about 1.8 mmHg per g/day: a 5 g/day reduction in the community would shift mean SBP by about 9 mmHg — clinically large at population level. Judge size against what matters clinically, not against 0.05.
:::

# Topic 6 — Confounding and adjustment {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## What is a confounder?

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'nodeSpacing': 40, 'rankSpacing': 70, 'padding': 14, 'htmlLabels': false}, 'themeVariables': {'fontSize': '22px', 'fontFamily': 'Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif'}}}%%
flowchart LR
  A["Age / BMI<br/>(confounders)"] --> S["Salt intake<br/>(exposure)"]
  A --> B["Systolic BP<br/>(outcome)"]
  S ==>|"the effect we want"| B
  classDef conf fill:#fdebd0,stroke:#e67e22,stroke-width:2px;
  classDef exp fill:#d6eaf8,stroke:#3498db,stroke-width:2px;
  classDef out fill:#fadbd8,stroke:#e74c3c,stroke-width:2px;
  class A conf; class S exp; class B out;
```

::: {.key}
A **confounder** is associated with the exposure **and** the outcome, and is not on the causal path between them. Ignoring it **mixes** its effect into the crude estimate.
:::

## In our data: older, heavier people eat more salt

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| fig-height: 4.4
cc |> select(salt_g, sbp, age, bmi) |>
  pivot_longer(c(age, bmi), names_to = "confounder", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(value, salt_g)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .25, colour = col_blue) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = col_red, formula = y ~ x) +
  facet_wrap(~ confounder, scales = "free_x", labeller = as_labeller(c(age = "Age (years)", bmi = "BMI (kg/m²)"))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Salt (g/day)")
```

::: {.fragment}
Age and BMI also raise SBP directly. So part of the crude salt–SBP slope is **really age and BMI**.
:::

## Crude vs adjusted β

```{r}
m_crude <- lm(sbp ~ salt_g, data = cc)
m_adj   <- lm(sbp ~ salt_g + age + bmi + sex + residence + education +
                tobacco + alcohol + phys_act, data = cc)

c(crude = coef(m_crude)[["salt_g"]], adjusted = coef(m_adj)[["salt_g"]])
100 * (coef(m_crude)[["salt_g"]] - coef(m_adj)[["salt_g"]]) / coef(m_crude)[["salt_g"]]   # % change
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.key}
The salt β shrinks from **`r round(b_c, 1)`** to **`r round(b_a, 1)`** mmHg per g/day — **`r round(100*(b_c-b_a)/b_c)`%** of the crude association was confounding. (Rule of thumb: ≥10% change ⇒ the variable matters as a confounder.)
:::
:::

## Which variable moved it? Add them one at a time

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
steps <- list(
  "Crude"        = "salt_g",
  "+ age"        = c("salt_g", "age"),
  "+ BMI"        = c("salt_g", "age", "bmi"),
  "+ sex"        = c("salt_g", "age", "bmi", "sex"),
  "+ residence, education" = c("salt_g", "age", "bmi", "sex", "residence", "education"),
  "+ tobacco, alcohol, activity" = c("salt_g", "age", "bmi", "sex", "residence", "education",
                                     "tobacco", "alcohol", "phys_act")
)
path <- map_dfr(steps, \(v) tidy(lm(reformulate(v, "sbp"), cc), conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term == "salt_g"), .id = "model") |>
  mutate(model = fct_inorder(model))

ggplot(path, aes(estimate, fct_rev(model))) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), colour = col_navy) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "β for salt (mmHg per g/day), 95% CI", y = NULL)
```

## Interpreting adjusted coefficients

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
tbl_regression(m_adj, intercept = FALSE) |> bold_labels()
```

::: {.notes}
Every coefficient is "holding the other variables in the model constant". Read the salt row: about 1.8 mmHg per g/day. Then age: about 0.6 mmHg per year. BMI: about 0.9 mmHg per kg/m² — so roughly 4.5 mmHg per 5 units.
:::

## "Holding the others constant"

::: {.key}
**Adjusted β for salt = `r round(b_a, 1)`:** *compare two people of the **same age, BMI, sex, residence, education, tobacco, alcohol and activity** — the one who eats 1 g/day more has, on average, `r round(b_a, 1)` mmHg higher SBP.*
:::

::: {.incremental}
- "Adjusted for" ≠ "removed": the model only removes **measured** confounders, assuming a **linear, additive** structure
- Unmeasured confounding (family history, stress, measurement error in salt) can remain
:::

## Confounding can even reverse a story: education

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
edu <- bind_rows(
  Crude    = tidy(lm(sbp ~ education, cc), conf.int = TRUE),
  Adjusted = tidy(m_adj, conf.int = TRUE),
  .id = "model") |> filter(str_detect(term, "^education")) |>
  mutate(term = str_remove(term, "education"), term = factor(term, c("Primary", "Secondary", "Graduate+")))

ggplot(edu, aes(estimate, term, colour = model)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), position = position_dodge(.5)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Crude = col_red, Adjusted = col_blue)) +
  labs(x = "Difference in SBP vs 'No schooling' (mmHg)", y = NULL, colour = NULL)
```

::: {.fragment}
Crude: "educated people have lower SBP". Adjusted for **age** (older adults have less schooling *and* higher SBP) the gradient largely disappears.
:::

# Dummy coding {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Categorical predictors become 0/1 columns

```{r}
model.matrix(~ education, data = cc) |> head(6)
```

::: {.incremental}
- A variable with **k levels** → **k − 1 dummy variables**
- The omitted level is the **reference** (all dummies = 0) — here "No schooling"
- Each coefficient = **difference vs the reference**, holding the other variables constant
:::

## Interpreting each level

```{r}
tidy(m_adj, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(str_detect(term, "education|phys_act|sex")) |>
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ signif(.x, 2)))
```

::: {.incremental}
- `sexMale` = **`r round(coef(m_adj)[["sexMale"]], 1)`** → men have `r round(coef(m_adj)[["sexMale"]], 1)` mmHg higher mean SBP than women (reference), all else equal
- `phys_acthigh` = **`r round(coef(m_adj)[["phys_acthigh"]], 1)`** → high vs **low** activity (the reference)
- Always state the **reference category** when you report a categorical β
:::

## Changing the reference: `relevel()`

```{r}
cc$education2 <- relevel(cc$education, ref = "Graduate+")
m_adj2 <- lm(sbp ~ salt_g + age + bmi + sex + residence + education2 +
               tobacco + alcohol + phys_act, data = cc)
tidy(m_adj2) |> filter(str_detect(term, "education")) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2)))
c(salt_before = coef(m_adj)[["salt_g"]], salt_after = coef(m_adj2)[["salt_g"]])
```

::: {.fragment}
Same model, same fit, same salt β — only the **comparison** changes. Choose a reference that is **large**, **clinically meaningful** (e.g. lowest-risk or "usual" group) and **stated in the table footnote**.
:::

# Model-building strategies {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Four ways to choose covariates {.smaller}

| Strategy | Idea | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **DAG / theory-driven** | Choose covariates from causal knowledge *before* looking at p-values | ⭐ **Recommended** |
| **Purposeful selection** | Screen, fit, drop, re-check change in β | Acceptable if confounding-focused |
| **Forward / backward / stepwise (AIC)** | Let an algorithm add and drop terms | ⚠️ Exploration only |
| **Univariable p < 0.2 screening** | Keep what is "significant" alone | ⚠️ Avoid (Session 6) |

## Purposeful selection (Hosmer–Lemeshow)

::: {.incremental}
1. Fit each variable **alone**; keep those clinically important or with a liberal p (≈ 0.20–0.25)
2. Fit the **multivariable** model with all of those
3. Remove variables that are non-significant **and** whose removal changes other β by **< 10–20%**
4. **Add back** any variable that changes the exposure β by ≥ 10–20% (confounder)
5. Check **linearity** and plausible **interactions**
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.warn}
It is driven by **change in the exposure β**, not only p-values — better than stepwise, but still data-driven.
:::
:::

## DAG / theory-driven selection — recommended

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'nodeSpacing': 25, 'rankSpacing': 55, 'padding': 12, 'htmlLabels': false}, 'themeVariables': {'fontSize': '20px', 'fontFamily': 'Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif'}}}%%
flowchart LR
  Age --> Salt
  Age --> BMI
  Age --> SBP
  Res["Residence"] --> Salt
  Res --> BMI
  BMI --> Salt
  BMI --> SBP
  Sex --> BMI
  Sex --> SBP
  Edu["Education"] --> SBP
  Age --> Edu
  Salt ==> SBP
  Tob["Tobacco,<br/>alcohol, activity"] --> SBP
  classDef conf fill:#fdebd0,stroke:#e67e22,stroke-width:2px;
  classDef exp fill:#d6eaf8,stroke:#3498db,stroke-width:3px;
  classDef out fill:#fadbd8,stroke:#e74c3c,stroke-width:3px;
  classDef prec fill:#eaf2f8,stroke:#85929e,stroke-dasharray: 4 3;
  class Age,BMI,Res,Sex,Edu conf; class Salt exp; class SBP out; class Tob prec;
```

::: {.notes}
This DAG is the team's causal story, drawn before analysis. Orange = confounders to adjust for. Dashed = risk factors for the outcome only: adjusting for them improves precision but is not needed for confounding. DAGs are assumptions — state them, defend them, and show sensitivity to alternatives.
:::

## How theory chooses the model

::: {.incremental}
- **Adjust for** common causes of exposure and outcome (age, sex, residence, BMI-as-confounder, education)
- **Add** outcome-only risk factors (tobacco, alcohol, activity) for **precision**
- **Do not adjust** for **mediators** (on the path salt → … → SBP) or **colliders**
- **Pre-specify** the model in your protocol; report it **regardless of p-values**
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.good}
That is exactly the "adjusted" model we have been fitting — chosen from the **diagram**, not from the p-values.
:::
:::

## Automated selection: how `step()` works

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
::: {.key}
**Forward**

start empty → add the term that lowers **AIC** most → stop when none helps
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.key}
**Backward**

start full → drop the term whose removal lowers **AIC** most → stop when none helps
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.key}
**Both (stepwise)**

at each step consider **adding or dropping** → stop when AIC cannot improve
:::
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
AIC = fit penalised for number of parameters; **lower is better**. (Same data, same rows in every model!)
:::

## `step()` in R — forward

```{r}
m_null <- lm(sbp ~ 1, data = cc)
m_full <- lm(sbp ~ salt_g + age + bmi + waist + sex + residence + education +
               tobacco + alcohol + phys_act, data = cc)

fwd <- step(m_null, scope = formula(m_full), direction = "forward", trace = 0)
fwd$anova |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 1)))
```

## `step()` in R — backward and both

```{r}
bwd  <- step(m_full, direction = "backward", trace = 0)
both <- step(m_full, direction = "both",     trace = 0)
bwd$anova |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 1)))
```

## Do they agree?

```{r}
sel <- list(forward = fwd, backward = bwd, both = both, full = m_full)
map_dfr(sel, ~ {
  tl <- attr(terms(.x), "term.labels")
  tibble(n_terms = length(tl), AIC = round(AIC(.x), 1),
         salt_b = round(coef(.x)[["salt_g"]], 2),
         adiposity_kept = paste(intersect(c("bmi", "waist"), tl), collapse = " + "))
}, .id = "strategy")
```

::: {.fragment}
**Forward kept `waist`; backward and both kept `bmi`** — near-duplicates. Which "wins" is a coin flip, not science.
:::

## Why automated selection is problematic

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.bad}
**1. Biased β** — selected variables look stronger than they are (winner's curse)
:::
::: {.bad}
**2. Too-narrow CIs and p-values too small** — they ignore that you searched
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.bad}
**3. Unstable** — a different sample selects different variables
:::
::: {.bad}
**4. Ignores confounding logic** — can drop a confounder, keep a mediator, or pick `waist` over `bmi` by chance
:::
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
Let us *see* 1–3 in our data.
:::

## Demo 1: step() on pure noise

```{r}
set.seed(1)
noise <- as_tibble(matrix(rnorm(nrow(cc) * 20), ncol = 20, dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("z", 1:20))))
d_n   <- bind_cols(cc |> select(sbp, salt_g, age, bmi), noise)
kept  <- step(lm(sbp ~ ., data = d_n), trace = 0)

tidy(kept) |> filter(str_detect(term, "^z")) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))
```

::: {.fragment}
Twenty **random-number** variables, nothing to find. `step()` kept **`r sum(grepl("^z", names(coef(kept))))`** of them, one with **p = `r round(min(summary(kept)$coefficients[grepl("^z", rownames(summary(kept)$coefficients)), 4]), 3)`**. A thesis table built this way reports "significant" noise.
:::

## Demo 2: the selection changes with the sample

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
set.seed(42)
vars <- c("salt_g", "age", "bmi", "waist", "sex", "residence", "education", "tobacco", "alcohol", "phys_act")
B <- 100
res <- map(seq_len(B), \(i) {
  bs <- cc[sample(nrow(cc), replace = TRUE), ]
  mm <- step(lm(reformulate(vars, "sbp"), bs), trace = 0)
  list(sel = vars %in% attr(terms(mm), "term.labels"),
       alc = if ("alcoholYes" %in% names(coef(mm))) coef(mm)[["alcoholYes"]] else 0)
})
freq <- tibble(variable = vars, selected = rowMeans(sapply(res, `[[`, "sel")))

ggplot(freq, aes(selected, reorder(variable, selected))) +
  geom_col(fill = col_blue) + geom_vline(xintercept = c(.5, 1), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "% of 100 bootstrap samples in which backward step() kept the variable", y = NULL)
```

::: {.notes}
Bootstrap = resample the same 550 people with replacement and rerun the whole procedure. Variables such as BMI, alcohol and education flip in and out; residence and waist are rarely selected. A "final model" from one run is one draw from this distribution.
:::

## Demo 3: the β after selection is distorted

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.8
b_alc <- sapply(res, `[[`, "alc")
tibble(beta = b_alc) |>
  ggplot(aes(beta)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = col_blue, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = coef(m_full)[["alcoholYes"]], colour = col_red, linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(x = "β for alcohol across 100 step() runs (0 = dropped)", y = "bootstrap samples")
```

::: {.fragment}
Red line = full-model β (`r round(coef(m_full)[["alcoholYes"]], 1)`). Alcohol survived in **`r sum(b_alc != 0)`** of 100 runs; **when kept, its average β was `r round(mean(b_alc[b_alc != 0]), 1)`** — inflated; when dropped it is **0**. One "final" model hides all of this, hence **overly narrow CIs**.
:::

## A defensible workflow

::: {.incremental}
1. **Think first** — draw the DAG; list confounders; fix the model in the protocol
2. **Fit** crude and adjusted models; report **both** (`tbl_merge`)
3. **Check assumptions** (Session 4)
4. **Sensitivity**: alternative covariate sets (e.g., swap BMI ↔ waist)
5. Use `step()`, if at all, **only to explore** — and say so
:::

## Self-check quiz (1/6) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s3q1", "The salt coefficient has p = 0.0003. Which statement is correct?",
         c("There is a 0.03% chance that the null hypothesis is true",
           "Data this extreme would be rare if the true β were exactly 0",
           "Salt explains 99.97% of the variation in systolic pressure",
           "The effect of salt on blood pressure is clearly clinically important"), answer = 2,
         explain = "A p-value is the probability of data this extreme IF H0 (and the model) were true. It says nothing about effect size or clinical importance.")
```

## Self-check quiz (2/6) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s3q2", "The salt β falls from 3.4 (crude) to 1.8 after adjusting for age, BMI and others. What does this mainly suggest?",
         c("Salt has no effect on systolic pressure at all",
           "Part of the crude association was due to confounding",
           "The adjusted model contains too many variables",
           "The crude model must have contained a calculation error"), answer = 2,
         explain = "Age and BMI relate to both salt intake and SBP, so part of the crude association was theirs. Adjusting removes measured confounding.")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s3q3", "In the adjusted model with low activity as the reference, phys_acthigh = −5.0. What does this mean?",
         c("Each additional hour of weekly activity lowers a person's SBP by 5.0 mmHg on average",
           "High-activity adults average 5.0 mmHg less SBP than low-activity ones, others equal",
           "Physical activity reduces systolic pressure by 5% in everyone who exercises more",
           "High-activity adults are five times as common as low-activity adults in the sample"), answer = 2,

```

## Self-check quiz (4/6) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("s3q4", "Which statement about stepwise (AIC) selection is TRUE?",
         c("It identifies the model with the most plausible causal structure in the data",
           "The final p-values and CIs ignore the search, so they look too optimistic",
           "It tends to pick the same variables in each resample of the dataset",
           "It can never remove a variable that confounds the exposure-outcome link"), answer = 2,
         explain = "After selection the usual SEs ignore the data-driven search: estimates are biased away from 0, CIs are too narrow and the chosen set is unstable.")
```

## Self-check quiz (5/6) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_fill("s3q5", "An algorithm starts from an intercept-only model, adds the variable that most improves AIC at each step, and stops when none helps. What is this strategy called? (one word)",
          accept = c("forward", "forward selection"),
          explain = "Forward selection adds terms; backward elimination starts full and drops terms; stepwise can do both.")
```

## Self-check quiz (6/6) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_fill("s3q6", "With low activity as reference, phys_actmoderate = −3.4 and phys_acthigh = −5.0. How many mmHg lower is mean SBP in the high group than in the moderate group, all else equal? (1 decimal)",
          accept = c("1.6", "-1.6", "−1.6"),
          explain = "Both coefficients are differences from the same reference, so high versus moderate is −5.0 − (−3.4) = −1.6 mmHg.")
```

## Score and take-home

**Your score: <span class="quiz-score"></span>**

::: {.incremental}
- **p** answers "could this be chance?"; **CI** shows size and precision; ask "is it clinically meaningful?"
- **Confounding**: compare crude vs adjusted β (≥10% change matters)
- **Dummy coding**: k − 1 columns, each vs the **reference** — always name it
- **Choose covariates from theory (DAG)**, not from p-values; `step()` is exploration only
:::
